newsitem.title: USA: Fed official warns consumers on spending, debt.
newsitem.headline: Fed official warns consumers on spending, debt.

text.p: As upbeat consumers flock to shopping malls this holiday season, a Federal Reserve official, sounding a bit like the Grinch at Christmas, warned of dangers if they keep racking up huge credit-card debts.

Fed Governor Lawrence Lindsey, in a speech on Thursday to a consumer group, said Americans are saddled with record levels of debt -- including not only their credit-card balances, but also mortgages and auto loans.
The bottom line is that consumers are spending more money than they are taking in, he said.
"Roughly for every extra $1 we're earning, we're spending $1.10," Lindsey said, adding that this troubling situation could not continue and may push more households to the brink of bankruptcy.
Already this year, the annual bankruptcy rate has passed the one million mark for the first time in history, he noted.
In his speech, the Fed governor made no specific prognostications about the current holiday spending season or its impact on household debt.

So far though, retailers are reporting rather brisk sales. That, combined with consumers' tendency to pile on credit-card debt this time of year, could compound the problems for those who are already over-extended, some economists warned.
"It may not be a tremendous Christmas season but it will be a good Christmas season," said economist Kathryn Kobe of Joel Popkin and Co.

A heightened sense of job security amid low unemployment has lifted consumers' spirits, making them more apt to spend, Kobe said. "Consumers are not watching every penny so they will be using their credit cards."

Ronald Wilcox, professor of marketing and retail pricing at Carnegie Mellon University, agreed that Christmas purchases will probably bloat credit-card balances in the short-run. But he said many card holders will likely attempt to chip away at those balances shortly after the holiday spendng season ends.
"It has been a trend that people are paying down their credit card debts," Wilcox said.
Concerning household debt levels, Lindsey said the biggest problem appears to be among those in the middle- to upper-middle income brackets.
Many wealthy households, with incomes over $100,000 a year, have paid off what they owed.
While the expansion of credit to families in the lower-middle bracket has boosted their debt, debt-to-income ratios have shot up for those earning $50,000 to $100,000 a year.

According to Lindsey, between 1992 and 1995, consumer debt ratios for the middle- to upper-middle income bracket have risen nearly six percentage points and mortgage ratios have surged almost 10 percentage points.

"Think about what this means," Lindsey told the consumer group. "For a couple making $60,000, essentially they've added $6,000 to their home equity line. They've added perhaps $2,500 to their auto debt and $1,100 on their credit card -- all in the three years 1992 to 1995."
Still, Lindsey was not predicting a dire outcome.
He said the banking sector was healthy and that credit-card issuers appeared to be showing more caution in the face of bad consumer debts they have been forced to write off.
Also, Lindsey forecast moderate growth in real disposable income and a slower pace of increases in consumer spending, which could enable more people to start paying off debt.
The Fed governor said major economic problems can be avoided so long as banks and consumers do not overreact.
His advice to both: "Be cautious, be prudent, don't make any sudden decisions but be aware of what the facts are."
